analysis.one_liner: Bans raising prices of essential goods more than 10% during federally declared emergencies.
analysis.headline: Introduced as COVID-19 price gouging spread, the bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died without a vote or a single action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared emergency, the bill would make it illegal to sell essential goods — food, water, medicine, gas, masks and other protective equipment — for more than 10% above what similar sellers charged in the 120 days before the emergency was declared. Sellers could avoid liability if the higher price simply reflected their own added costs. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rule in court. It was introduced on April 3, 2020, weeks into pandemic-era shortages, and never received any action beyond its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers buying essentials during a declared emergency — a hurricane, wildfire, or pandemic — who would be protected from sudden 10%-plus markups on goods they cannot go without, such as water, medicine, gasoline, and protective masks. State attorneys general would gain a new federal backstop to sue price gougers and recover money for residents.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to sell or offer any consumer good during a declared emergency, and for 30 days after, at more than 10% above the price charged by similar sellers in the 120 days before the declaration [S2][S3].

Covered goods include food, water, gasoline, prescription and over-the-counter medications, and personal protective equipment, plus anything public health officials deem vital during a public health emergency [S3].

Sellers who raised prices only because their own costs rose are protected: an increase directly attributable to added costs of goods, labor, or materials is not a violation, nor is a price within 10% of the seller's cost plus its customary markup [S2][S3].

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban with the same powers it has under the FTC Act, and state attorneys general could sue in federal or state court to stop violations, collect civil penalties, and win restitution or damages for their residents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers of essential goods — grocery stores, pharmacies, gas stations, and suppliers of protective equipment — would bear the risk of civil penalties and lawsuits if they raised prices beyond the 10% band during an emergency, and would bear the recordkeeping burden of proving any increase reflected their own higher costs.

drawbacks.text: A rigid 10% cap keyed to pre-emergency prices may not fit every shortage: sellers argued then, as now, that higher prices ration scarce goods and signal suppliers to send more, and a hard cap can empty shelves faster or push goods to gray-market resellers outside the law's reach.

The cost-based safe harbor turns on proving 'additional costs' and a 'customary markup,' which invites disputes over accounting and paperwork that would fall hardest on small sellers without compliance staff [S2][S3].

The ban lasts only through an emergency declaration plus 30 days, so it would not touch the ordinary-time pricing it leaves 'best to the marketplace,' and it applies only to federally declared emergencies rather than all severe local price shocks [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: at the exact moments people cannot shop around — during a declared disaster or pandemic — the bill removes the ability to profit from their lack of alternatives, while carving out honest cost increases. The tradeoffs are design limits rather than fatal flaws: a flat 10% band can misfire in genuinely supply-constrained markets, and the enforcement machinery leans on after-the-fact lawsuits rather than immediate relief. On balance it is a consumer protection that would have bitten mainly in emergencies, when the stakes for households are highest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee took no further action on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act on April 3, 2020, weeks into the COVID-19 emergency, with ten Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retailers and suppliers of essential goods are better off: the bill never advanced, so no federal limit on emergency markups was created, and no FTC or state enforcement power over emergency pricing was added. Consumers who faced pandemic-era price spikes got no new protection.

for.name: Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 3, 2020, during the COVID-19 emergency, and sought a federal anti-price-gouging standard enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 3, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress, keeping the bill off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; with Democrats holding the House majority, the lack of committee action, not a floor vote, decided the outcome [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Grocery, convenience, pharmacy and gas retailers
industries.note: The bill would cap their emergency prices at 10% above pre-emergency levels across essentials including food, gasoline, and medicine, with civil penalties and state AG lawsuits for violations. Their gain from the bill's death was continued freedom to raise prices at the moments consumers have least ability to shop around.

industries.industry: Personal protective equipment and medical supply suppliers
industries.note: Masks, gloves, and other protective gear are expressly covered, and 2020 saw sharp markups on exactly these goods; the bill would have exposed suppliers and resellers to FTC and state enforcement. Its death left emergency pricing of protective equipment to market forces.

The ban applies to 'any seller,' reaching online listings that drove much pandemic-era gouging, a new compliance exposure; but the 10% band and cost safe harbor would still allow moderate increases. The bill's death left marketplace pricing unregulated at the federal level.
